items.title: Frank Turek Fights ‘War on Reality,’ Offers Warning for America
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "Dystopia"
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Apologist Frank Turek is on a mission to tackle the “war on reality,” warning Americans face a “dystopia” if the nation continues marching toward Marxism.

Turek’s new book, “The War on Reality Workbook: Recovering Truth in a World That Celebrates Lies,” is being released as the nation recently remembered the one-year anniversary of the assassination of conservative and Christian commentator Charlie Kirk.

The apologist told CBN News he and his coauthor, Phoenix Hayes, dedicated the book to Kirk, calling the late Turning Point USA founder a “warrior for reality.”

Turek broke down the current state of culture and decried many elements that simply make no logical — or biblical — sense.

“Abortion is healthcare; we’re pulling baby body parts out of women, and we’re calling that health care,” he said. “That’s a war on reality, and Charlie was a casualty in the war on reality. But, thankfully, since he was a believer, all the murderer was able to do is change his address.”

Turek continued, “He’s absent from the body, present with the Lord, and we remain behind, still engaged in fighting for reality when so many forces are fighting against.”

items.title: Christian Singer Colton Dixon Says Charlie Kirk’s Assassination ‘Changed’ Him
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "It gave me a new outlook on things."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Christian singer-songwriter Colton Dixon said the assassination of Charlie Kirk and the government’s restrictive response to the COVID-19 pandemic “changed” him.

Dixon, 35, told CBN News seeing Kirk murdered for exercising his right to free speech pushed him “to seek truth harder.”

“I feel like, just for a lot of people, whether you believed in what Charlie stood for or not, just for a lot of people, it was, like, it just — I don’t know, it changed me,” said Dixon. “It was just, like, ‘Wow.’ [It] gave me a new outlook on things, even just to seek truth harder.”

The up-and-coming generation, he added, aren’t taking things at face-value anymore, regardless of the source. “They’re seeking truth for themselves,” he explained.

As a Christian recording artist, Dixon said he believes he has found the answer: “The answer’s Jesus.”

The recent spate of culture-defining events have, according to the “Build a Boat” singer, “anchored my feet down in my beliefs so that I’m not going to be pushed around by a little Chihuahua who might bark louder.”

“I kind of even really figured out why I believe what I believe,” he said. “[B]ecause again, it’s just COVID and just all these different things, they’re trying to get you to do different things and I’m like, ‘OK, why aren’t we just going to do it?’ Let’s figure out why so we’re not just being stubborn [and] hardheaded.”

“We open up God’s Word, we pray, we seek godly wisdom, and then we come to the conclusion, ‘Oh, this is why,'” Dixon said. “So now I just feel more steadfast in why I believe what I believe.”

As he’s ruminated on his convictions in recent years, Dixon has become noticeably more comfortable creating edgier content — at least edgier for the status quo in the contemporary Christian music world.

The “American Idol” alumnus just released a new song, “Bones,” based on the Old Testament passage of Ezekiel 37, chronicling the story of the prophet being transported to a valley filled with dry bones. God asked whether the bones could live and then commanded Ezekiel to prophesy over them. As the prophet began speaking promises to the bones, they assembled and were covered in flesh. Then a second prophecy called breath to fill their lungs and they became a living army standing to their feet.

Dixon said the song is “straight from Scripture,” recalling reading the biblical account and feeling “super inspired” and “like God gave me revelation” about speaking “over the dead things in your life.”

During a time of year when most of American culture is fixated on death from a secular perspective, Dixon saw an opportunity to flip the script around Halloween with a biblical understanding of death.

“What if we could … take this passage that already theatrically lines up with a lot of the visuals of skeletons — that’s what this whole passage was, it was a valley of dry bones, the bones rattling, coming together, flesh coming upon the bones, it was like zombies out there, you know, in Ezekiel 37,” he reflected.

That passage of Scripture, Dixon emphasized, shows a biblical interpretation of death, which, for the Christian, he said, is “just a little blip on the timeline of what our lives look like.”

He said, “For the rest of the world, death is the final word. … That’s the period. Life after death is this big mystery. But for a believer, death is not the final word; the cross —what Jesus did on the cross — is the final word, and not only that, but three days later, Him resurrecting from the grave so that we could spend eternal life with Him in heaven. … Death can be a scary thing to talk about, but as a believer, I don’t think it should be.”

The song — and its music video, which is set at night in a graveyard — is certainly unorthodox in its approach, but it paints a clear picture to the world that this life is not all there is. It also tells the story of spiritual power, a nod toward Romans 8:11, where Paul wrote, “The Spirit of God, who raised Jesus from the dead, lives in you. And just as God raised Christ Jesus from the dead, he will give life to your mortal bodies by this same Spirit living within you” (NLT).

“I think that this song is … a kick in the pants for sideline Christians, where I’ve found myself before,” said Dixon. “It’s time to start using the spiritual authority that we have as believers and not just talk the talk, but walk it, as well.”

In fact, for Dixon, it was his wife Annie’s certainty about spiritual authority that led him to do some self-reflection.

“I found myself being so in awe of [my wife] that that was her first response [to pray and speak over things],” he said. “But then also going, ‘Why isn’t that mine?’ You know? If I’m really going to be the best spiritual leader of our house, I need to stop kicking my feet up and actually get in the game and start doing this for real.”

items.title: Franni Cash on Leaving the Family Band, Her Solo Debut and Growing Up in a Cult
items.author: Cameron Strang
items.summary: Franni Cash was about 13 when she says the community her family belonged to officially became a cult. She was 17 when her family left it. She told RELEVANT that her parents joined after their marriage hit a rough patch and a friend suggested counseling. The therapist they saw, she said, was “dangero
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Franni Cash was about 13 when she says the community her family belonged to officially became a cult. She was 17 when her family left it.

She told RELEVANT that her parents joined after their marriage hit a rough patch and a friend suggested counseling. The therapist they saw, she said, was “dangerously smart” and used people’s vulnerabilities “to kind of tether loyalty to himself.” Counseling sessions became Bible studies with other families, and then she says they were told they no longer needed church. Eventually the leader declared himself their spiritual father and warned that anyone who broke covenant with him would be cut off, and women who disagreed with their husbands were said to have “the Jezebel spirit.”

“It just became so far away from the truth,” Cash said.

She kept a diary about how strange it all felt. The leader found it and burned it. She was 14. “From that place I pushed it down,” she said. “I can’t question it and can’t voice this anymore.”

Her family left in the middle of her senior year of high school, after an article exposed years of alleged fraud and sexual allegations tied to the leader. She remembers her parents telling the kids in their bedroom.

“It was like this weight flew off my shoulders,” she said. Then came a harder year, when she feared the curses and watched her brothers struggle. “I didn’t know if I was gonna make it. I really mean that.”

Her parents put the family in therapy immediately. Talk therapy alone didn’t work for her, because she was still so brainwashed she didn’t know what she could say. EMDR and brainspotting did. She has been in consistent therapy for ten years now and says talking about the cult no longer stings.

“I’ve had to grieve them being susceptible to something so harmful,” she said of her parents. “But right off the bat, they got themselves in therapy.”

She describes her healing journey as medicine and scripture working together. “You can’t just slap a Bible verse on it,” she said. “Scripture is so powerful, but sometimes you don’t know how to absorb it until you can do some surgery.”

The family’s first song came a year and a half after they left, and it became We the Kingdom. Cash said the band was a place where she felt understood, because her family were the only people who could laugh at the jokes instead of being horrified. She also says they were trauma bonded, and that she needed to learn who she was on her own. She left the band, and says she and her family are now the closest they’ve ever been, “from a health and respect” place that “doesn’t feel enmeshed.”

Her solo debut, Here I Am, takes its title from a lyric she and her father, producer and songwriter Ed Cash, wrote together for the song “The Real Thing”: Here I am, I made it through. The page is burned, but this story is not over.

Here I Am was also going to be the title of an album she planned at 16, in the middle of everything. “Now here I am, kind of on the other side of healing,” she said.

Getting there meant relearning music. A friend, the writer Paul Duncan, told her she needed to “date music like you would your spouse,” meaning listen to records she loved as a kid with no goal. She was driving on the Pacific Coast Highway when U2’s “Where the Streets Have No Name” came on.

“It was like I heard music for the first time,” she said. She has since been listening to Marvin Gaye’s What’s Going On, Al Green, Elton John, Casey Musgraves, John Mayer and Linkin Park’s Hybrid Theory.

Her view of God changed too. “I just really thought that God was this angry man upstairs,” she said.

She remembers being told to get off the worship stool because she wasn’t “anointed enough.” Then she met what she calls the real Jesus. “He was so loving. And gracious with me,” she said. “It changed everything.”

When we asked what she’d say to someone inside a controlling church, her answer was short. “Leave. You’re free to. God is gonna protect you.”

She said that when you’re afraid of hurting people by leaving, “when something is the best decision for you, it’ll be the best decision for them too.”

And she said questioning is allowed. “It’s okay to question your faith, and it’s okay to take down the bricks that need to go,” she said. “The chief cornerstone is worth keeping around because he’s pretty awesome.”

items.title: Stoker’s ‘Dracula’ and True Deliverance from Evil
items.author: Matthew Malone
items.summary:
Matthew Malone

In Stoker's "Dracula" lies a deep exploration into the nature of evil, the limitations of reason and science, and the indispensable power of Catholicism to confront and overcome supernatural evil.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Matthew Malone

Dracula is a name that has struck fear into the heart of Western culture for over a century. Dracula’s story has been told and retold innumerable times through novels, comic books, and perhaps most notably, films like Nosferatu (1922), Dracula (1931) and Bram Stoker’s Dracula (1992). Much of the enduring mythology of the modern vampire owes its origins to Bram Stoker, whose masterful synthesis of folklore, history, and Gothic literature gave the world its most iconic incarnation of the parasitic undead. Beneath the bloody horror and predatory eroticism lies a deeper exploration into the nature of evil, the limitations of reason and science, and the indispensable power of Catholicism to confront and overcome supernatural evil. 

Abraham “Bram” Stoker was born on November 8, 1847, in the Clontarf suburb of Dublin, Ireland. Bedridden by an unknown illness until the age of seven, he developed a dark turn of mind, encouraged by his mother’s tales of Ireland’s cholera epidemic when people were mistakenly buried alive. After miraculously recovering, Bram excelled as an athlete at Trinity College and graduated in 1870. He began publishing fiction like The Crystal Cup (1872) and horror novella The Chain Of Destiny (1875). Notably, Stoker also wrote The Snake’s Pass (1890), which was partially inspired by the legend of St. Patrick expelling the serpents from Ireland. 

Stoker’s career changed dramatically after he favorably reviewed Henry Irving’s performance in Shakespeare’s Hamlet. The young Bram became Irving’s devoted associate, and in 1878, Irving appointed Stoker as manager of London’s prestigious Lyceum Theatre. Stoker held the position for twenty-seven years and became acquainted with Oscar Wilde, Arthur Conan Doyle, and W. B. Yeats. That same year, he married Florence Balcombe, who later converted to Catholicism in 1904. Stoker himself remained an Irish Protestant throughout his life with interests extending into mesmerism and Freemasonry.

Stoker’s Count Dracula evokes a long literary tradition of diabolical figures from Dante’s Lucifer to Milton’s Satan to Goethe’s Mephistopheles. The aristocratic vampire archetype was first developed by Lord Byron’s personal physician John William Polidori and published in his tale, The Vampyre (1819). It was adapted into a play by James Robinson Planché and had its debut at Lyceum Theatre, the very theatre Stoker later managed. 

Yet the novel’s origins may lie in a far more intimate source. Some scholars have linked Dracula’s conception to a nightmare Stoker experienced in 1890. In the dream, Stoker was confronted by seductive and vampiric women who violently attempted to kiss his throat, only to be summoned away by a commanding and mysterious figure with a booming voice saying, “This man belongs to me!” The vision would later be recalled in the novel through Jonathan Harker’s confrontation with Dracula’s brides. The extent to which this chilling nightmare inspired the novel is uncertain, yet it offers a fascinating glimpse into the haunted imagination from which Dracula was born. 

Later in 1890, Stoker travelled to Whitby, the Yorkshire seaside town that would become a key setting in the novel. There, he accumulated stories from the locals about ghostly shipwrecks and made extensive notes of the tombstones in St. Mary’s churchyard. He became a regular visitor to the local library where he read Emily Gerard’s The Land Beyond the Forest (1888), detailing the superstitions and mysterious folklore of Transylvania. The book documented local tales of “nosferatus” (undead vampires) and the means to repel and kill them, such as garlic, wooden stakes, extracting the heart, or decapitating the corpse—methods Stoker later incorporated into Dracula. 

Stoker’s historical research appeared to have led him to Vlad III, referred to as Vlad the Impaler or Vlad Dracula, the fifteenth-century ruler of Wallachia known for his extreme cruelty and violence. Stoker’s research included William Wilkinson’s An Account of the Principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia (1820), linking the name Dracula with the Romanian word for “dragon” or “devil.” In the novel, the character Van Helsing speculates whether the Count and Vlad are the same person, and he references the aforementioned The Land Beyond The Forest, saying, “[Count Dracula] must indeed have been that Voivode Dracula who won his name against the Turk. . . . If it be so, then he was no common man: for in that time, and for centuries after, he was spoken of as the cleverest and the most cunning, as well as the bravest of the sons of the land beyond the forest.” In Dracula, Bram Stoker masterfully synthesized his nightmarish subconscious, the aristocratic vampire tradition, Transylvanian folklore, and the legend of Vlad the Impaler into a dark convergence of historical violence, predatory eroticism, and supernatural evil. 

Dracula is an epistolary novel told through diary entries, letters, telegrams, and newspaper articles. The story begins with Jonathan Harker, a naive English lawyer who travels to Transylvania to assist the mysterious Count Dracula in purchasing property in London. At the Count’s remote castle in the Carpathian mountains, Harker discovers that Dracula is a nosferatu, an undead vampire who feeds upon human blood. Dracula leaves for England, where he pursues Harker’s loved ones. Harker joins forces with Dutch professor Abraham Van Helsing to hunt and kill Dracula.

As the novel progresses, the characters appeal to medicine for a cure to vampirism yet they discover that reason and science are insufficient to comprehend or defeat the power of Dracula. Their confrontation demands a deeper understanding of the spiritual world, where faith and God’s power become indispensable weapons. This tension is revealed in an exchange between the physician Dr. Seward and Professor Van Helsing, who challenges Seward’s conviction that reality is limited by scientific explanation: 

(Van Helsing:) You are a clever man, friend John; you reason well, and your wit is bold; but you are too prejudiced. You do not let your eyes see nor your ears hear, and that which is outside your daily life is not of account to you. Do you not think there are things which you cannot understand, and yet which are; that some people see things that others cannot? . . . It is the fault of our science that it wants to explain it all; and if it does not explain it, then it says there is nothing to explain. . . . There are always mysteries in life. 

[ . . .]

(Seward:) Do you mean to tell me that Lucy was bitten by such a bat; and that such a thing is here in London in the nineteenth century? 

(Van Helsing:) My thesis is this: I want you to believe. 

(Seward:) To believe what? 

(Van Helsing:) To believe in things that you cannot. 

Van Helsing exposes the limits of science to explain all phenomena—in this case, an undead vampire—yet he does not reject reason outright. From a Catholic perspective, the distinction is crucial. Faith is not the abandonment of reason, nor the belief in what is untrue, but the fulfillment of reason and the intellect’s ascent toward truth transcending mere sensory perception. The characters’ confrontation with the embodiment of evil cannot be resolved by reason alone; it demands the language, rituals, and sacraments of the Catholic tradition. In Stoker’s nightmarish vision, Dracula is more than a monster; he is the abominable counterfeit of eternal life, an inversion of light and holiness, a parasitic creature that feeds on the lives of others for pleasure and to sustain his power. 

As the story unfolds, the characters discover the extraordinary power of Catholic sacramentals and the Blessed Sacrament to repel the supernatural evil embodied by Count Dracula. In Chapter 1, Harker receives a crucifix from the local villagers as he journeys towards Dracula’s castle, a gesture of protection against the horrors awaiting him. In Chapter 16, Van Helsing repels the vampiric Lucy with a golden crucifix and uses the Blessed Sacrament to seal her tomb. Later, in Chapter 22, he places fragments of the Blessed Sacrament inside Dracula’s boxes of Transylvanian earth, sanctifying the soil and rendering it an unusable refuge for the vampire. Throughout Dracula, Stoker repeatedly demonstrates the power of Catholic objects and rituals to repel and protect from supernatural evil. Against the Count’s own satanic inversion of eternal life, the Blessed Sacrament stands athwart, confronting evil not through human reason alone but through the authority and power of God and his Church. 

The Church’s history of confronting supernatural evil dates back to Christ’s expulsion of demons in the Gospels, and the formal rites of exorcism developed and codified over the centuries. The Second Council of Nicaea (787 AD) defended the veneration and holiness of sacred images, determining that

“the honour rendered to an image passes to its prototype” (CCC 2132). This principle is crucial to understanding the power of the sacred in Dracula. When the Count retreats from a crucifix, he is not confronted by merely wood and metal but by the truth the image points toward: Christ, whose death and resurrection have conquered sin, death, and evil. 

The Blessed Sacrament takes this a step further. Whilst the crucifix is a sacred image pointing to Christ, the Blessed Sacrament is Christ himself, “For in the blessed Eucharist is contained the whole spiritual good of the Church, namely Christ himself, our Pasch” (CCC 1324). When Van Helsing wields the Blessed Sacrament against Dracula, he confronts evil’s embodiment with the living presence of Christ, the source of all love, beauty, and truth. This reflects the Catholic conviction that there is no greater power on earth than the Body and Blood of Christ. 

While Count Dracula is the satanic inversion of eternal life, Christ is the very source. Dracula must consume the blood of the living to sustain his existence, while Christ gives his blood to gain eternal life for others. Dracula perverts love to possess and dominate, while Christ’s love liberates. Dracula’s immortality is a curse, but Christ promises eternal life with God in heaven. Dracula preserves himself at the expense of others, while Christ offers himself as the salvation for others. Dracula embodies death, but Christ entered into death and conquered it through his resurrection. 

Dracula remains a quintessential and ubiquitous figure in modern culture synonymous with evil, vampirism, death, and dread. The novel offers a vision of the ultimate victory of light over darkness and the power of Catholicism to confront diabolical malevolence and sin. Stoker’s Dracula serves as a cautionary tale against the satanic promise of eternal life through profane and unholy means. It reminds us that Christ, who is “the way, the truth and the life,” is the source of eternal life and our hope of deliverance from evil.

items.title: Thursday, October 29, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus compares himself to a mother hen who longs to gather her chicks under her wing.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
Ephesians 6:10-20

Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his power. Put on the whole armor of God, so that you may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. For our struggle is not against enemies of blood and flesh, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers of this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places. Therefore take up the whole armor of God, so that you may be able to withstand on that evil day, and having done everything, to stand firm. Stand therefore, and fasten the belt of truth around your waist, and put on the breastplate of righteousness. As shoes for your feet put on whatever will make you ready to proclaim the gospel of peace. With all of these, take the shield of faith, with which you will be able to quench all the flaming arrows of the evil one. Take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

Pray in the Spirit at all times in every prayer and supplication. To that end keep alert and always persevere in supplication for all the saints. Pray also for me, so that when I speak, a message may be given to me to make known with boldness the mystery of the gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains. Pray that I may declare it boldly, as I must speak.

Psalm
Psalm 144:1b, 2, 9-10

Blessed be the Lord, my rock,
    who trains my hands for war, and my fingers for battle;
my rock and my fortress,
    my stronghold and my deliverer,
my shield, in whom I take refuge,
    who subdues the peoples under me.
I will sing a new song to you, O God;
    upon a ten-stringed harp I will play to you,
the one who gives victory to kings,
    who rescues his servant David.

Gospel Reading
Luke 13:31-35

At that very hour some Pharisees came and said to him, “Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you.” He said to them, “Go and tell that fox for me, ‘Listen, I am casting out demons and performing cures today and tomorrow, and on the third day I finish my work. Yet today, tomorrow, and the next day I must be on my way, because it is impossible for a prophet to be killed outside of Jerusalem.’ Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often have I desired to gather your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing! See, your house is left to you. And I tell you, you will not see me until the time comes when you say, ‘Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus compares himself to a mother hen who longs to gather her chicks under her wing. As the theologian N. T. Wright points out, this is much more than a sentimental image. It refers to the gesture of a hen when fire is sweeping through the barn. In order to protect her chicks, she will sacrifice herself, gathering them under her wing and using her own body as a shield.

On the cross, Jesus used, as it were, his own sacrificed body as a shield, taking the full force of the world’s hatred and violence. He entered into close quarters with sin (because that’s where we sinners are found) and allowed the heat and fury of sin to destroy him, even as he protected us.

With this metaphor in mind, we can see, with special clarity, why the first Christians associated the crucified Jesus with the suffering servant of Isaiah. By enduring the pain of the cross, Jesus did indeed bear our sins; by his stripes we were indeed healed.
